sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: firm ABS pressure versus pumping failed brakes, stop versus turn versus speed up, injury versus stuck versus movable crash scenes, private versus government property thresholds, and the vehicle-failure procedures
Confusable pairs among crash-avoidance, after-crash and vehicle-failure rules, where similar emergencies call for opposite actions; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec09-R01 | anchor: A01
Tapping the brake three or four times is a warning signal to drivers behind you, not an emergency stopping method. [A01]
Why it matters: group signaling; confusable warning taps versus stopping.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec09-R02 | anchor: A01
Emergency braking with ABS uses firm, continuous pressure, not repeated pumping of the pedal. [A01]
Why it matters: group braking; confusable ABS pressure versus pumping; misconception pump ABS brakes.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec09-R03 | anchor: A01
The handbook example for speeding up is a vehicle about to strike your car from the side or the rear, and you slow down again once that danger has passed. [A01]
Why it matters: group crash avoidance; confusable speed up versus stop or turn; difficulty medium.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec09-R04 | anchor: A01
Turning away from one collision is only half the job, because you must then keep control so you do not cause a second one. [A01]
Why it matters: group crash avoidance; misconception the swerve ends the danger.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec09-R05 | anchor: A02
With an injury or death you leave the vehicles where they are, but with no injuries and a drivable car you move it off the road. [A02]
Why it matters: group crash scene; confusable injury versus no-injury scene.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-R06 | anchor: A02
With no injuries but a car that cannot move, you call 911, follow the directions given and stay away from traffic, whereas a drivable car is moved off the road. [A02]
Why it matters: group crash scene; confusable stuck versus movable vehicle.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-R07 | anchor: A02
The police reporting threshold is $1,000 for property damage in general but only $200 for damage to government property such as signs or guardrails. [A02]
Why it matters: group crash reporting; confusable private versus government property.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-R08 | anchor: A02
A crash needs a police report even without injuries or major damage when a vehicle cannot be moved or a driver appears impaired. [A02]
Why it matters: group crash reporting; misconception only injury crashes are reported.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-R09 | anchor: A03
When the brakes fail, pumping the pedal comes first and the parking brake second, and the parking brake is released if it causes a skid. [A03]
Why it matters: group vehicle failures; confusable failed brakes versus ABS braking.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-R10 | anchor: A03
A stuck gas pedal is handled by shifting into neutral, while a blowout is handled by easing off the gas and slowing gradually. [A03]
Why it matters: group vehicle failures; confusable stuck pedal versus blowout.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-R11 | anchor: A03
When the engine dies you keep the key in the on position, and only with a stuck gas pedal does the handbook say to turn the engine off, once you are safely off the road. [A03]
Why it matters: group vehicle failures; confusable engine failure versus stuck pedal; difficulty hard.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-R12 | anchor: A03
The handbook warns that the steering wheel will be hard to turn after the engine stops, so expect extra effort while pulling over. [A03]
Why it matters: group vehicle failures; misconception steering failure.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0052]
